| Measurement | Value | Unit | Note |

| **Laser Power (measured)** | 0.0 | W | Zero value – no power output detected |

All listed values are present (none are missing) and are reported as zero.
Does the zero laser-power reading prove a hardware failure or a defective part? Explain possible causes and what additional evidence would be needed to distinguish them

**Is the zero laser‑power reading a sign of a hardware fault or a defective part?** | What the reading tells us | Implications | |---------------------------|--------------| | **Commanded power = 100 W, measured power = 0 W** | The laser system is **not delivering any electrical/optical power** at the point of measurement. This is a direct indication that the laser output is absent or severely reduced. A part that is physically present cannot cause the laser to “turn off”; it can only affect the *resulting* melt‑pool geometry, not the power itself. | ### Possible causes | Category | Likely causes (based on the data) | How they would affect the reading | |----------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------| | **Laser hardware / drive** | • Laser diode or fiber failure
• Optic element (lens, mirror, window) damaged or mis‑aligned
• Power supply or driver fault
• Software/firmware error that bypasses power delivery | These would stop or reduce the actual laser power, yielding the 0 W measurement you see. | | **Control/command chain** | • Faulty communication between the host and the laser controller
• Incorrect command packet or corrupted power setting | The controller may receive the 100 W command but fail to convert it to hardware output, again showing 0 W. | | **Measurement error** | • Faulty DAQ or sensor mis‑calibrated
• The power measurement probe is not connected or defective | If the probe itself is faulty, it could read 0 W even when the laser is on. | | **Process / part‑related** | • The part’s geometry or material could theoretically absorb the laser energy quickly, but that would still produce a measurable power spike at the source. | Unlikely to cause a *zero* reading; more likely it would show a low or irregular power profile, not 0 W. | ### What evidence would help decide | Evidence needed | What it would confirm | |-----------------|-----------------------| | **External optical power meter** | Direct measurement of laser output power; if it also reads near zero, it confirms a hardware fault. | | **Laser driver fault logs** | Presence of fault codes (e.g., “Laser off”, “Optic failure”) would indicate a hardware issue. | | **Optical inspection** | Checking mirrors, lenses, and the laser head for damage or mis‑alignment. | | **Power supply monitoring** | Verifying that the laser’s electrical supply is within specifications. | | **Run a different build or part** | If the laser works on a different part, the issue is likely part‑specific; if it still fails, the laser hardware is suspect. | | **DAQ/DAQ‑to‑laser interface diagnostics** | Checking that the command signal is actually reaching the laser controller. | | **Cross‑check with another sensor** | Using a second, independent power sensor to rule out measurement error. | ### Bottom line A zero reading in the *measured* laser power, while the command is 100 W, almost always points to a **hardware or control‑chain failure** rather than a defect in the part. The part might cause problems later (e.g., no melt pool), but it cannot make the laser output zero. Gathering the additional diagnostics listed above would let you distinguish between an actual hardware fault and any spurious measurement artefact.
What should the operator check next before changing any process settings? Base your guidance on the available evidence and state what remains uncertain.

**What the operator should check next**

| Priority | Action | Why it matters | What is still uncertain |
|----------|--------|----------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | **Confirm the laser is actually off** by using an external optical power meter or the laser controller’s built‑in diagnostic screen. | If the external meter also reads ~0 W, the problem is a real hardware or control failure. | If the external meter reads a non‑zero value, the DAQ (your “measured” instrument) may be faulty. |
| 2 | **Verify the laser driver and power supply** (voltage, current, fault‑codes). | Many LPBF systems will shut the laser down if a safety interlock or power‑supply fault occurs. | The exact fault code may still be unknown without the vendor‑specific diagnostics. |
| 3 | **Check the communication link** between the build controller (host) and the laser driver. | A corrupted command packet could cause the laser to ignore the 100 W setting. | Whether the link is physically intact (cable, connectors) versus a software‑level issue. |
| 4 | **Inspect the optics** (lens, mirrors, windows) for dust, mis‑alignment or damage. | Even a small mis‑alignment can drop the optical power to zero. | Whether any optical element is out of focus or physically damaged—requires visual inspection or laser‑beam profiling. |
| 5 | **Run a quick diagnostic test** on a simple part (or a calibration “test track”) that doesn’t involve complex geometry. | If the laser works on a minimal build, the issue may be part‑related (e.g., mis‑placed part causing a safety shut‑off). | The test still won’t confirm if a subtle part geometry is the cause of the zero‑power readout. |
| 6 | **Cross‑check the DAQ signal** (laser‑power channel) with a second sensor or the same sensor on a different channel if possible. | Rules out a defective DAQ sensor or wiring. | It remains possible that the sensor is mis‑calibrated, but a second sensor would confirm. |

---

### What remains uncertain

| Issue | Why it is uncertain | What would resolve the uncertainty |
|-------|---------------------|-------------------------------------|
| **Is the zero power due to a DAQ sensor failure or real laser shutdown?** | The DAQ reads 0 W, but we have no independent measurement yet. | External power meter or laser‑driver diagnostics. |
| **Is there a software or firmware fault that is overriding the commanded power?** | The command value is 100 W but not reflected; could be a code bug. | Review controller logs/fault codes; check firmware version. |
| **Could the part geometry or placement be causing an automatic safety shut‑off?** | A mis‑aligned or unsupported part could trigger a safety interlock. | Verify part placement, inspect for any interlock activations. |
| **Is the laser physically damaged (optics, diode, etc.)?** | Zero power could be due to a broken laser diode or mis‑aligned optics. | Physical inspection, laser‑beam profiler, vendor support. |

---

**Next step for the operator:**  
Start with the simplest, most definitive check—measure the laser output with an independent optical power meter (or view the laser controller’s status screen). If the external measurement still shows zero power, proceed to inspect the driver/fault codes and optics. Only after confirming the laser hardware is functional should you look at process‑related adjustments.
